codes.label: Rent as share of income
codes.definition: Whether the rent fits within a sustainable share of income, judged against take-home pay rather than gross, and how much margin it leaves for savings, emergencies, debt and other costs.

codes.label: Monthly savings gap
codes.definition: How much the cheaper option saves each month and year, and what that money could do (build an emergency fund, pay down debt, fund goals) if the extra cost of the pricier option isn't worth it.

codes.label: Upfront cash and emergency cushion
codes.definition: How much of current savings would be consumed by the deposit, first month's rent and setup costs, and whether enough reserve remains to survive a gap or surprise expense.

codes.label: Paycheck timing and income stability
codes.definition: Whether the first paycheck, start date, probation period or other income uncertainty could leave a shortfall, and how confident the person is in steady income.

codes.label: True total monthly cost
codes.definition: Comparing options on all-in cost, including utilities, internet, renter's insurance, transit or fuel, furnishings, parking and fees, rather than headline rent alone.

codes.label: One-time moving and setup costs
codes.definition: The deposits, movers, utility setup, lost work time, furniture and overlapping rent involved in relocating, and how long the savings take to recoup them.

codes.label: Lease length and flexibility
codes.definition: The tradeoff between a longer fixed lease (price certainty, but exposure if plans change and early-termination penalties) and shorter or month-to-month terms that preserve the option to leave.

codes.label: Rent stability and future increases
codes.definition: Whether a fixed-term lease locks in a predictable rate against likely further increases at the current place, so the real cost gap depends on expected future rents.

codes.label: Commute time, cost and reliability
codes.definition: The daily time, fatigue, fare or fuel, and dependability of getting to work in each option, including weather, schedules and late or early hours.

codes.label: Career effects of location
codes.definition: Whether living near work makes it easier to stay late, attend informal events and build relationships that could shape early career growth.

codes.label: Deadline pressure and verification
codes.definition: Treating a short deadline as pressure to be tested: asking for an extension, confirming refundability and lease terms, and vetting the landlord and unit before committing money.

codes.label: Negotiating with the current landlord
codes.definition: Whether the rent increase, lease term or terms of renewal can be negotiated, using comparable listings or vacancy costs as leverage, before deciding to leave.

codes.label: Privacy, social life and wellbeing
codes.definition: How the living arrangement affects privacy, rest, loneliness and the chance to build a local social network, depending on temperament and the stress of a new city.

codes.label: Long-term plans and time horizon
codes.definition: How long the person expects to stay, and whether future job, family, education or home-buying plans make a longer commitment more or less sensible.

codes.label: Credit and approval requirements
codes.definition: Whether credit history, rental record, income verification or employment paperwork will affect approval or required deposits for a given landlord.

codes.label: Middle-path alternatives
codes.definition: Exploring options between the two choices, such as a shorter or negotiated lease, a cheaper or closer place, a sublet, or starting temporarily in the flexible option.

codes.label: Family support network and childcare
codes.definition: The value of nearby relatives providing free childcare and help, and the cost and strain of replacing that support if the family moves farther away.

codes.label: Children's school and routine disruption
codes.definition: How changing school districts or moving affects the children's friendships, academic continuity, services, activities and adjustment, including timing within the school year.

codes.label: School quality and fit research
codes.definition: Investigating the actual quality, programs, special-needs support and fit of the new district for these particular children rather than relying on reputation.

codes.label: Parents' commute and daily logistics
codes.definition: How a move changes both parents' travel to work, school drop-offs and pickups, activities and errands, in time, fuel and schedule flexibility.

codes.label: Home and neighborhood quality
codes.definition: Comparing the condition, size, layout, safety, amenities and landlord reliability of the current home versus the alternative, including neighborhood ties and community.

codes.label: Disruption and stress of moving
codes.definition: The non-financial burden of packing, time off work, updating addresses and helping family adjust, weighed against the stress of staying under a higher rent.

codes.label: Employer benefits and assistance
codes.definition: Whether an employer offers relocation help, a signing bonus, a transit or housing stipend, or flexibility that could offset upfront or ongoing costs, which can be checked by asking HR before deciding.

codes.label: Own spending habits and behavioral tendencies
codes.definition: How the person's own tendencies, such as spending freely in a new place, mean that a cheaper option may protect them better, or that a cognitive bias like anchoring distorts how fair a price increase feels.

codes.label: Local rental supply and search difficulty
codes.definition: Whether comparable homes are scarce or plentiful in the area, since leaving the current place could lead to a harder, more rushed search later.

codes.label: Buying instead of renting
codes.definition: Whether rising rent makes homeownership worth exploring, including whether savings, credit and long-term goals could support a down payment and fit the person's plans.

codes.label: Aligning partners' priorities
codes.definition: When more than one adult is affected, discussing and reconciling each person's preferences about money, stability, schools, family closeness and commute so the choice is made jointly before any deadline.

codes.label: Values-based tradeoff and affordability headroom
codes.definition: When both options are financially feasible, deciding which factors the household values most, such as savings versus family support or stability, since the choice turns on quality of life rather than survival.
